A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Switch SAE work. Their text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including the additional analyses in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE training experiments, reconstruction and sparsity comparisons, feature-geometry analyses, and automated interpretability results in Figures 1 and 3–6.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds a load-balancing hyperparameter sweep and evaluations at additional activation sites and on Gemma 2 2B.

M1.justification: The TopK experts, single-expert routing, probability-weighted reconstruction, and combined reconstruction/load-balancing objective remain unchanged. Equations 1–4 and the default alpha=3 are retained; the new sweep evaluates the existing method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates GPT-2 small layer-8 residual-stream activations. Appendix B in v2 substantially broadens the activation populations tested by adding attention and MLP outputs, residual activations at additional layers, and Gemma 2 2B residual activations. No additional text corpus or downstream task is identified.

E2.justification: The corresponding main comparisons retain ReLU, Gated, and TopK SAEs; the new appendix comparisons use the existing TopK baseline. The changed ReLU citation does not establish a different comparator. Newly discussed dictionary-learning and MoE methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: The main 100K-step, batch-size-8192 protocol is retained. Added experiments introduce a controlled alpha sweep and fixed-width comparisons at k=64 with eight experts, widths of 24,576 or 65,536, and fraction of variance explained alongside loss recovered. These are protocol extensions, not demonstrated reruns of the original experiments. Appendix B inconsistently names GPT-2 layer 12 where Table 1 lists layer 10.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.2 and Figure 7 test sensitivity to the load-balancing coefficient across eleven values from 0.001 to 100, using 16 and 32 experts at fixed width and sparsity. This focused analysis supports the existing alpha=3 choice. The previous duplication, specialization, and t-SNE analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 6 retains the same evaluation of 1,000 random features with 95% confidence intervals. v2 introduces no additional seed information, repeated-run counts, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures; the new sweep and table report point estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 7 and Table 1 add substantive results, including a stronger performance penalty at some non-residual sites. Table 1 reports TopK/Switch loss recovered of 0.888/0.701 for GPT-2 layer-2 MLP outputs, versus 0.997/0.996 for that layer's residual stream, and 0.991/0.989 for Gemma residual activations. These are newly reported settings, not before-and-after performance changes. Figure 3 retains its underlying values while replotting loss recovery as 1−FLR.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds a short computational-cost derivation: active parameter counts are 2Md for TopK and dN+2Md/N for Switch, yielding the approximate FLOP reduction when router costs are negligible. The architecture and loss equations are unchanged, and no new theorem or proof framework is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, five contribution statements, and central conclusion retain the same claims: Switch SAEs improve reconstruction versus compute while preserving feature interpretability. The new evidence and qualifications do not redefine the proposed contribution or its principal novelty claim.

C2.justification: v1 mainly identifies the fixed-parameter performance penalty. v2 substantially expands applicability qualifications: attention and MLP sites suffer larger penalties, only a simple MoE architecture is tested, and downstream steering or circuit discovery remains unevaluated and may be complicated by duplication. Section 4.1 also newly extrapolates from the unchanged scaling plot that the fixed-width penalty might become negligible at larger scales.

D1.justification: The original training-details appendix is preserved as A.1. v2 adds the alpha search grid, explicit parameter/FLOP accounting, router parameter proportions, and settings for the supplementary evaluations. Initialization, normalization, optimizer instructions, and the code-access URL remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens the research context through early MoE history, classical sparse coding and dictionary learning, and earlier sparse/k-sparse autoencoders. Section 2.3 now contrasts SAEs with methods such as optimal directions and K-SVD. The limitations also position future extensions relative to GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert-choice routing.

P1.justification: v2 adds localized explanations, standardizes loss-recovery terminology as FLR, expands related work, and separates the limitations discussion. Appendix A becomes an implementation section with three subsections, followed by new Appendix B. The main section sequence, abstract, and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 7 and Table 1, revises Figure 3 to display logarithmic 1−FLR, expands captions for Figures 1 and 4, and makes localized diagram and placement adjustments. Existing scaling, geometry, and interpretability graphics are retained rather than replaced by new results.

improvement.justification: The added evaluations improve on v1's single-site evidence by exposing meaningful attention/MLP limitations, while the alpha sweep and FLOP accounting better support experimental choices. Expanded limitations improve transparency. The gains remain bounded: the supplementary comparison uses one sparsity and one Gemma site, its layer labels conflict between Appendix B and Table 1, and the favorable large-scale extrapolation remains speculative.
